```{r}
#| echo: false
#| message: false
library(tidyverse)
library(openintro)
library(patchwork)
options(scipen = 999)

source("R/plot-normal.R")

green <- hds_colors[["green"]]
yellow <- hds_colors[["yellow"]]
pink <- hds_colors[["pink"]]

theme_set(theme_minimal(base_size = 22))

# A normal curve with no y-axis (we only care about the shape and areas)
theme_curve <- theme(axis.text.y = element_blank(),
                     axis.title.y = element_blank(),
                     panel.grid.major.y = element_blank(),
                     panel.grid.minor = element_blank())

# Small static normal curve with a shaded area (for pictures, not for students)
shade_normal <- function(mean, sd, from = -Inf, to = Inf, title = NULL, breaks = NULL) {
  curve <- tibble(x = seq(mean - 4 * sd, mean + 4 * sd, length.out = 500),
                  y = dnorm(x, mean, sd))
  area <- curve |> filter(x >= from, x <= to)
  p <- ggplot(curve, aes(x, y)) +
    geom_area(data = area, fill = pink, alpha = 0.9) +
    geom_line(color = green, linewidth = 1.3) +
    labs(x = NULL, title = title) +
    theme_curve
  if (!is.null(breaks)) p <- p + scale_x_continuous(breaks = breaks)
  p
}

# Heights (cm) of physically active adults in the bdims data
women <- bdims |> filter(sex == 0)
men <- bdims |> filter(sex == 1)
```

# Normal distribution {.inverse background-color="#A51C30"}

## A familiar shape

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-height: 5
#| fig-width: 14
#| fig-align: center
#| fig-alt: "Three histograms side by side. Left: heights of 260 physically active women, centered near 165 cm. Middle: heights of 247 physically active men, centered near 178 cm. Right: heights of 435 NBA players, centered near 201 cm. All three are roughly symmetric and bell shaped."
hist_plot <- function(data, var, title) {
  ggplot(data, aes({{ var }})) +
    geom_histogram(binwidth = 2.54, fill = green, color = "white") +
    labs(x = "Height (cm)", y = NULL, title = title)
}
(hist_plot(women, hgt, "Active women") |
   hist_plot(men, hgt, "Active men") |
   hist_plot(nba_heights, h_meters * 100, "NBA players")) &
  theme(plot.title = element_text(size = 20), axis.text.y = element_blank())
```

Many variables have a symmetric, bell-shaped distribution.

<small>Data: [bdims](https://openintrostat.github.io/openintro/reference/bdims.html) and [nba_heights](https://openintrostat.github.io/openintro/reference/nba_heights.html) in the `openintro` package.</small>

## Normal distribution

The __normal distribution__ is a symmetric, bell-shaped curve. It is completely described by two numbers:

- its __mean__: where the center is,
- its __variance__, or __standard deviation__ (the square root of the variance): how spread out it is.

. . .

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-height: 3.4
#| fig-width: 11
#| fig-align: center
#| fig-alt: "Histogram of the heights of active women with a smooth green normal curve on top. The curve, with mean 165 cm and standard deviation 6.5 cm, follows the shape of the histogram closely."
ggplot(women, aes(hgt)) +
  geom_histogram(aes(y = after_stat(density)), binwidth = 2.54, fill = "gray80", color = "white") +
  stat_function(fun = dnorm, args = list(mean = mean(women$hgt), sd = sd(women$hgt)),
                color = green, linewidth = 1.6) +
  labs(x = "Height (cm)") +
  theme_curve
```

Heights of active women are approximately normal with mean `r round(mean(women$hgt))` cm and standard deviation `r round(sd(women$hgt), 1)` cm.

## Changing the mean

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-height: 4
#| fig-width: 11
#| fig-align: center
#| fig-alt: "Three normal curves with the same standard deviation, 6.5, centered at 150, 165, and 180. Changing the mean slides the curve left or right without changing its shape."
tibble(m = c(150, 165, 180)) |>
  expand_grid(x = seq(120, 210, length.out = 500)) |>
  mutate(y = dnorm(x, m, 6.5), m = factor(m)) |>
  ggplot(aes(x, y, color = m)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1.5) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("gray40", green, pink), name = "mean") +
  labs(x = NULL, title = "Same standard deviation (6.5), different means") +
  theme_curve
```

. . .

The mean moves the curve left and right.

## Changing the standard deviation

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-height: 4
#| fig-width: 11
#| fig-align: center
#| fig-alt: "Three normal curves all centered at 165 with standard deviations 4, 6.5, and 12. The curve with standard deviation 4 is tall and narrow; the one with 12 is short and wide."
tibble(s = c(4, 6.5, 12)) |>
  expand_grid(x = seq(120, 210, length.out = 500)) |>
  mutate(y = dnorm(x, 165, s), s = factor(s)) |>
  ggplot(aes(x, y, color = s)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1.5) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("gray40", green, pink), name = "standard\ndeviation") +
  labs(x = NULL, title = "Same mean (165), different standard deviations") +
  theme_curve
```

. . .

The standard deviation makes the curve narrower or wider. The total area under the curve is always 1, so a narrower curve is taller.

## SAT scores

From here on, we will use SAT scores as our example.

We will assume that total SAT scores have

- mean 1000
- standard deviation 200

and SAT Math scores have mean 500 and standard deviation 100.

These values are close to, but not the same as, recent SAT scores: we altered them to make mental math easier.

```{r}
#| echo: false
sat_mean <- 1000
sat_sd <- 200
```

## Notation

$$\text{random variable} \sim N(\text{mean}, \text{variance})$$

. . .

::: {.stat-callout .example}
**Example**

Let $X$ be the total SAT score of a randomly selected test taker.

$$X \sim N(1000, 200^2)$$

is read "$X$ is normally distributed with mean 1000 and variance $200^2$." The standard deviation is 200 and the variance is $200^2 = 40{,}000$.
:::

## Many ways to say the same thing

All of these mean the same thing:

- $X$ is normally distributed with mean 1000 and variance 40,000.
- $X$ is normally distributed with mean 1000 and standard deviation 200.
- $X \sim N(1000, 40{,}000)$
- $X \sim N(1000, 200^2)$
- $X \sim \text{Normal}(\text{mean} = 1000, \text{sd} = 200)$

## Careful!

::: {.stat-callout .note-tip}
**Note**

Some books and some software put the standard deviation (not the variance) as the second number. In R, `pnorm()`, `qnorm()`, and `rnorm()` all use the standard deviation:

`pnorm(1200, mean = 1000, sd = 200)`

Always check whether the second number is the standard deviation or the variance. Writing it as $200^2$ makes it clear.
:::

## Reading the notation {.smaller}

::: {.stat-callout .exercise}
**Exercise**

For each normal distribution, find the mean, the variance, and the standard deviation.

a. $Y \sim N(10, 4)$
b. $Z \sim N(0, 1)$
c. $W \sim N(-3, 3^2)$
d. SAT Math scores have mean 500 and standard deviation 100.

Note: $N(0, 1)$ in (b) is called the standard normal distribution.
:::

## Not just for $X$ {.smaller}

The random variable on the left of $\sim$ can be many things.

| Notation | What is normally distributed? |
|-----------------------------|---------------------------------------------|
| $X \sim N(1000, 200^2)$ | a __random observation__ (in the population, and so also in a sample): the SAT score of one test taker |
| $\mu \sim N(7, 0.5^2)$ | a __random population parameter__: our belief about the mean hours of sleep of all Harvard students |

: What can be normally distributed: an observation or a population parameter

In a few weeks, we will see that a __random sample statistic__, like $\bar{X}$, can also be normally distributed.

. . .

This is why we say "mean" and "variance" for the two numbers in $N(\ , \ )$ rather than giving them their own symbols: sometimes the random variable itself is a mean, like $\mu$!

# Probability as area {.inverse background-color="#A51C30"}

## Area = probability

The total area under a normal curve is 1. The __probability__ that the random variable falls in an interval is the __area__ under the curve over that interval.

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-height: 3.4
#| fig-width: 14
#| fig-align: center
#| fig-alt: "Three normal curves for SAT scores, centered at 1000 with standard deviation 200. In the first, the area to the left of 800 is shaded, labeled P(X < 800). In the second, the area to the right of 1400 is shaded, labeled P(X > 1400). In the third, the area between 800 and 1400 is shaded, labeled P(800 < X < 1400)."
b <- c(400, 800, 1200, 1600)
(shade_normal(sat_mean, sat_sd, to = 800, title = "P(X < 800)", breaks = b) |
   shade_normal(sat_mean, sat_sd, from = 1400, title = "P(X > 1400)", breaks = b) |
   shade_normal(sat_mean, sat_sd, from = 800, to = 1400, title = "P(800 < X < 1400)", breaks = b)) &
  theme(plot.title = element_text(hjust = 0.5))
```

. . .

We will never calculate these areas by hand. We will use functions.

## The `plot_normal()` function

```{r}
#| eval: false
plot_normal(random_variable = "x",  # "x", "x_bar", "p", "mu", or "pi"
            mean = 1000,            # mean of the normal distribution
            sd = 200,               # standard deviation (or variance = 40000)
            lower = 800,            # shade from here...
            upper = 1400)           # ...to here
```

- It draws the normal curve with the random variable on the x-axis.
- It shades the area between `lower` and `upper` and writes the area under the plot.
- Leave out `lower` to shade everything below `upper`, and leave out `upper` to shade everything above `lower`.

## The `calc_prob_normal()` function

`plot_normal()` draws the picture. To get the probability as a number that you can use in your answers, use `calc_prob_normal()` with the same arguments:

```{r}
calc_prob_normal("x", mean = 1000, sd = 200, lower = 800, upper = 1400)
```

. . .

You can save it and use it with inline code:

```{r}
prob_800_1400 <- calc_prob_normal("x", mean = 1000, sd = 200, lower = 800, upper = 1400)
```

About `r round(prob_800_1400 * 100)`% of test takers scored between 800 and 1400.

## Area to the left

What is the probability that a randomly selected test taker scored below 800?

```{r}
#| fig-height: 3.6
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-align: center
#| fig-alt: "Normal curve for X with mean 1000 and standard deviation 200. The area to the left of 800 is shaded pink, and a yellow label below the curve reads Area = 0.1587. The title is P(X < 800)."
plot_normal("x", mean = 1000, sd = 200, upper = 800)
calc_prob_normal("x", mean = 1000, sd = 200, upper = 800)
```

## Area to the right

What is the probability that a randomly selected test taker scored above 1400?

```{r}
#| fig-height: 3.6
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-align: center
#| fig-alt: "Normal curve for X with mean 1000 and standard deviation 200. The area to the right of 1400 is shaded pink, and the label reads Area = 0.0228."
plot_normal("x", mean = 1000, sd = 200, lower = 1400)
calc_prob_normal("x", mean = 1000, sd = 200, lower = 1400)
```

## Area in between

What is the probability that a randomly selected test taker scored between 800 and 1400?

```{r}
#| fig-height: 3.6
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-align: center
#| fig-alt: "Normal curve for X with mean 1000 and standard deviation 200. The area between 800 and 1400 is shaded pink, and the label reads Area = 0.8186."
plot_normal("x", mean = 1000, sd = 200, lower = 800, upper = 1400)
```

## The 68-95-99.7 rule

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-height: 4.5
#| fig-width: 15
#| fig-align: center
#| fig-alt: "Three standard normal curves. The first shades the area within 1 standard deviation of the mean, labeled 68%. The second shades within 2 standard deviations, labeled 95%. The third shades within 3 standard deviations, labeled 99.7%. The x-axes are labeled mean minus 3 sd through mean plus 3 sd."
lab <- c("mean\n- 3 sd", "mean\n- 2 sd", "mean\n- 1 sd", "mean", "mean\n+ 1 sd", "mean\n+ 2 sd", "mean\n+ 3 sd")
rule_plot <- function(k, pct) {
  shade_normal(0, 1, from = -k, to = k, title = pct) +
    scale_x_continuous(breaks = -3:3, labels = lab, limits = c(-3.6, 3.6)) +
    theme(plot.title = element_text(hjust = 0.5, size = 30, face = "bold"),
          axis.text.x = element_text(size = 12))
}
rule_plot(1, "68%") | rule_plot(2, "95%") | rule_plot(3, "99.7%")
```

For __any__ normal distribution, about 68% of the values are within 1 standard deviation of the mean, 95% within 2, and 99.7% within 3.

## The 68-95-99.7 rule {.smaller}

**Exercise**

SAT total scores are approximately $N(1000, 200^2)$. Without using R, find the approximate probability that a randomly selected test taker scored

a. between 800 and 1200.
b. between 600 and 1400.
c. above 1400.
d. above 1000.

Then check (a) and (c) with `calc_prob_normal()`.
:::

## Match the picture {.smaller}

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-height: 6.5
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-alt: "Four normal curves labeled A, B, C, D, each centered at 1000 with standard deviation 200 and x-axis ticks at 800, 1000, and 1400. A shades the region to the right of 800. B shades the region to the left of 800. C shades the region between 800 and 1400. D shades the region to the right of 1400."
b <- c(800, 1000, 1400)
(shade_normal(sat_mean, sat_sd, from = 800, title = "A", breaks = b) |
   shade_normal(sat_mean, sat_sd, to = 800, title = "B", breaks = b)) /
  (shade_normal(sat_mean, sat_sd, from = 800, to = 1400, title = "C", breaks = b) |
     shade_normal(sat_mean, sat_sd, from = 1400, title = "D", breaks = b)) &
  theme(plot.title = element_text(size = 28, face = "bold"))
```

:::

::: {.column width="45%"}

::: {.stat-callout .exercise}
**Exercise**

$X \sim N(1000, 200^2)$. Match each picture to a probability.

1. $P(X < 800)$
2. $P(X > 1400)$
3. $P(X > 800)$
4. $P(800 < X < 1400)$

Then write the `plot_normal()` code for each.

## Exactly 1200?

::: {.stat-callout .discussion}
**Discussion**

$X \sim N(1000, 200^2)$. According to this model, what is the probability that a randomly selected test taker scored *exactly* 1200? Not 1200.1, not 1199.99999, but exactly 1200.000000...
:::

## Exactly 1200? - answer

__Answer: 0.__ The area of a single line under the curve is 0.

Just like the broken alarm last class: for a continuous random variable, we only ask about probabilities of __intervals__. This also means $P(X < 1200) = P(X \le 1200)$.

. . .

Real SAT scores are reported in steps of 10, so some students do score exactly 1200. The normal distribution treats scores as continuous: it is a model.

## Going backwards: `find_normal_value()`

Sometimes we know the area and want the value. What total SAT score does a test taker need to be in the top 10%?

```{r}
#| fig-height: 3.6
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-align: center
#| fig-alt: "Normal curve for X with mean 1000 and standard deviation 200. The area to the right of about 1256 is shaded pink, and the label reads Area = 0.1000."
find_normal_value("x", mean = 1000, sd = 200, area = 0.10, side = "above")
```

## Practice {.smaller}

::: {.stat-callout .exercise}
**Exercise**

SAT Math scores are approximately $N(500, 100^2)$.

a. What is the probability that a randomly selected test taker scored above 700 on SAT Math? Sketch the picture first, then use `plot_normal()` and `calc_prob_normal()`.
b. What is the probability that a randomly selected test taker scored between 400 and 600?
c. What SAT Math score separates the lowest 25% of test takers from the rest?
:::

## z-scores

A __z-score__ tells us how many standard deviations a value is away from the mean.

$$z = \frac{\text{value} - \text{mean}}{\text{standard deviation}}$$

. . .

::: {.stat-callout .example}
**Example**

A total SAT score of 1400: $z = \frac{1400 - 1000}{200} = 2$. The score is 2 standard deviations above the mean.
:::

. . .

If $X$ is normal, its z-score $Z = \frac{X - \text{mean}}{\text{standard deviation}}$ follows $N(0, 1)$, the __standard normal distribution__.

## Normal vs. standard normal

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-height: 5.4
#| fig-width: 13
#| fig-align: center
#| fig-alt: "Two normal curves of the same shape, one above the other. The top curve is the distribution of SAT total scores, N(1000, 200 squared), with x-axis ticks at 400, 600, 800, 1000, 1200, 1400, and 1600. The bottom curve is the standard normal distribution of z-scores, N(0, 1), with x-axis ticks at -3 through 3. In both, the area above the same point (1400 on the top, z = 2 on the bottom) is shaded, and both areas equal 0.023."
z_1400 <- (1400 - sat_mean) / sat_sd
top <- shade_normal(sat_mean, sat_sd, from = 1400,
                    breaks = sat_mean + (-3:3) * sat_sd,
                    title = expression("SAT total score:  " * X %~% N(1000, 200^2))) +
  labs(x = "X: SAT total score")
bottom <- shade_normal(0, 1, from = z_1400, breaks = -3:3,
                       title = expression("z-score:  " * Z %~% N(0, 1) * ", the standard normal distribution")) +
  labs(x = "Z: number of standard deviations from the mean")
(top / bottom) &
  theme(plot.title = element_text(size = 22), axis.text.x = element_text(size = 16),
        axis.title.x = element_text(size = 18))
```

A score of 1400 has $z = \frac{1400 - 1000}{200} =$ `r round(z_1400, 2)`. $P(X > 1400) = P(Z > `r round(z_1400, 2)`)$: converting to z-scores changes the numbers on the axis, not the shape or the areas.

## z-scores

::: {.stat-callout .exercise}
**Exercise**

SAT total scores are approximately $N(1000, 200^2)$ and SAT Math scores are approximately $N(500, 100^2)$.

Which is more unusual: a total SAT score of 1450 or an SAT Math score of 720?
:::

## Summary {.smaller}

- A normal distribution is described by its mean and variance: $N(\text{mean}, \text{variance})$. Check whether the second number is the standard deviation or the variance!
- Probability = area under the curve: `plot_normal()` draws the area, `calc_prob_normal()` calculates it (value → area), and `find_normal_value()` goes from area → value.
- The random variable can be a random observation ($X$) or a random population parameter that describes our uncertainty ($\mu$, $\pi$). In a few weeks: random sample statistics ($\bar{X}$, $p$).
- A z-score is the number of standard deviations a value is from the mean. z-scores follow the standard normal distribution, $N(0, 1)$.
